value.overview: The Ruddy Woodcreeper (Dendrocincla homochroa) is a medium-sized tropical woodcreeper in the ovenbird family, Furnariidae. Its rich rufous-brown plumage, long slightly curved bill, and habit of climbing along trunks distinguish it from many related species. It is mainly a bird of humid forest, where it searches bark and branches for insects. Individuals are often solitary, but they may join mixed bird groups or gather at army-ant swarms to catch fleeing prey.
value.classification: The Ruddy Woodcreeper belongs to the family Furnariidae and subfamily Dendrocolaptinae, the woodcreepers. Its scientific name is Dendrocincla homochroa.
value.identification: This woodcreeper is predominantly warm reddish or rufous brown, with relatively plain plumage and subtle variation between geographic forms. It has a long, narrow, slightly decurved bill, a stiff tail used for support, and the upright posture typical of trunk-climbing woodcreepers. It moves by hitching upward along trunks and large branches, often pausing to probe bark crevices. Its call is a useful identification clue because the bird can be difficult to detect inside dense forest.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Woodcreeper ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring on both Pacific and Caribbean slopes, although it is generally uncommon and less frequent in the lowest lowlands. It is found in humid evergreen forest, foothill forest, forest edges, mature secondary woodland, gallery forest, and partly open areas with trees. Costa Rican records extend from low elevations to roughly 1,350–1,500 meters, with especially suitable habitat in northern foothills and protected forest areas.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica; it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Its local movements may follow food availability, especially army-ant activity.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been documented mainly during May and June, although timing may vary by locality. The species nests in natural cavities, often in hollow trunks or bases of medium-sized trees, commonly a few meters above the ground. A Costa Rican observation reported two white eggs placed deep inside a vertical cavity. Little nest material may be used, though leaves, moss, wood chips, or other debris can occur. At least some nests may receive care predominantly from the female.
value.dietFeeding: The Ruddy Woodcreeper feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods found on or beneath tree bark. It climbs trunks, branches, and stems below the canopy, using its bill to investigate crevices and loose bark. Recorded prey includes insects and spiders. It is particularly associated with army-ant swarms, following moving ants and capturing insects that flee from the advancing swarm. Most feeding is solitary, but two or more birds may forage together at these temporary food concentrations.
value.behavior: This species is usually quiet and solitary while foraging, moving in short flights and upward climbs along trunks and branches. It may join mixed-species flocks, especially in forest understory and lower-canopy habitats. Army-ant swarms can attract several individuals and other insect-eating birds. The Ruddy Woodcreeper generally remains below the canopy and can be overlooked because its subdued plumage blends with tree bark. It may reuse a successful nest cavity in a later breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
